paper_title: ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are pushing conversational AI beyond multi-turn dialogues toward interactive assistants that can respond to diverse user requests, manage multiple concurrent tasks, and, when appropriate, proactively engage users as those tasks evolve [32, 56]. Bringing these capabilities into the physical world points toward long-standing vision of multimodal interactive AI [8, 19, 23]: systems such as JARVIS in Iron Man that continuously perceive streams of inputs while seamlessly interacting with human users, augmenting our ability to understand and act in complex, dynamic environments. Streaming video LLMs lie at the very heart of this vision. Recent models [4, 52, 53] can continuously process incoming video, reason about past observations [58], describe ongoing activities [5, 50], and monitor events as they occur. Yet todays streaming video LLMs remain largely passive, often responding to individual requests in isolation. They lack critical capability of interactive assistants: the ability to maintain and revise user tasks over time and proactively engage users as the video unfolds. This gap in interactivity substantially limits their potential as foundation for multimodal interactive AI. 1 Figure 1 ALIVE enables interactive streaming video understanding. Left: ALIVE monitors unfolding events, updates active tasks as user instructions change, and requests additional visual evidence when observations are insufficient. These examples illustrate Proactive Monitoring, Streaming Task Coordination, and Feedback-Seeking Interaction within continuous video stream. Right: Performance comparison on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench (EDP). In this work, we aim to transform streaming video LLMs from passive observers into interactive assistants. Given that modern video LLMs largely inherit the architecture of LLMs [25, 28], we ask key question: What data representation and learning framework can endow existing video LLMs with interactive capabilities? Addressing this question poses two challenges. First, constructing streaming interaction data requires aligning user requests, feedback, and assistant responses with the visual evidence available at each moment. Second, models must learn when and how to respond as context and task states evolve across multiple turns, where similar observations can call for different behaviors. To address these challenges, we first identify set of core capabilities required for interactive streaming video understanding and curate ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage post-training. We then develop learning framework that explicitly supports these capabilities. Contrastive SFT teaches strategy selection and response gating through controlled variations in interaction conditions and available evidence. Reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) further refines these behaviors by combining trajectory-level advantages with local advantages for strategy selection, task response, and critical silence. We also establish FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback-seeking interaction in streaming video LLMs. Our experiments show that an offline video LLM can indeed be transformed through post-training into capable interactive streaming video LLM. The resulting model preserves its ability to understand streaming it can simultaneously manage multiple video while acquiring substantially richer interactive behaviors: user-specified tasks, modify or cancel existing tasks, and proactively seek user feedback based on prior requests and events unfolding in the video. These results suggest path toward streaming video LLMs that do not merely watch and respond, but sustain ongoing interactions with users as the video streams. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate interactive streaming video understanding as set of core capabilities, including proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. Building on this formulation, we introduce ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage post-training, together with FSI-Bench, benchmark for evaluating feedback-seeking interaction. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model trained through contrastive SFT and reinforcement learning with BACA. We show that ALIVE achieves highly competitive performance across multiple streaming video benchmarks, preserving strong video understanding capabilities while substantially improving performance on interactive tasks. 2 Table 1 Comparison of streaming video training datasets. PM: Proactive Monitoring; STC: Streaming Task Coordination; FSI: Feedback-Seeking Interaction. /: explicit/no explicit support. Stage: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL). Scale follows each works counting unit (K = thousand).

sections.content: Streaming Video Models. Streaming video models process continuously arriving observations [20, 30] and determine when to respond [48]. VideoLLM-online couples temporally aligned dialogue with continuous inference [4], while Dispider separates perception, decision, and reaction for asynchronous interaction [37]. StreamBridge and AURA address sustained observation through memory and context management [31, 44]. JoyAI-VL-Interaction integrates silence, response, and delegation with an asynchronous background model [55]. ALIVE focuses on maintaining evolving user requests and resolving missing prerequisites through clarification, user execution, or continued monitoring. Post-training for Streaming Video Understanding. Streaming SFT learns response content and timing from temporally aligned dialogues, with supervision of response states and balancing of silence and speech [4, 31, 51]. Our contrastive SFT further supervises how interaction conditions and available evidence change the appropriate strategy and response gate. Beyond SFT, PPO [39] and GRPO [41] provide policy-optimization frameworks for LLM post-training. GiGPO [10] further addresses multi-turn credit assignment through episode-level and step-level advantages. In streaming video, MMDuet2 uses RL to improve response timing and correctness while penalizing repetition [46]. StreamPro uses GRPO with aggregated turn-level and trajectory-level rewards [22]. Our BACA combines trajectory-level advantages with local advantages over behavioral units for strategy selection, task response, and critical silence. Streaming Video Datasets and Benchmarks. Streamo-Instruct covers diverse streaming tasks, while ProAssist provides proactive assistantuser dialogues grounded in egocentric videos [51, 61]. StreamingBench and OVO-Bench evaluate online perception and temporal understanding [27, 29]. ProactiveVideoQA focuses on proactive response timing and quality, while IPIBench covers task updates and interleaved requests [24, 47]. Table 1 compares training datasets. ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K support two-stage training across monitoring, task coordination, and feedback seeking. FSI-Bench evaluates strategy selection and subsequent task completion when additional information, user action, or observation is required.

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.content: We consider streaming video model that continuously receives video observations and user utterances. At decision time t, its output depends only on the observed video prefix V1:t and the interaction history Ht, comprising received user utterances and prior model outputs. All mappings below describe causal rollouts: each output uses only information available at its own decision time. 3 passive streaming model executes fixed query Qt0 Ht issued at time t0: fθ(Qt0 , V1:t) (rt0, . . . , rt), (1) where (rt0 , . . . , rt) are responses from t0 to including the choice of remaining silence (SILENCE). This formulation covers immediate question answering and delayed or repeated event monitoring. Here, passive refers to executing fixed request without accommodating new requests or seeking additional user input, not to the absence of proactive responses. An interactive streaming model retains the same streaming capabilities as the passive setting, while supporting broader range of outputs and evolving interactions. Before receiving further user input, its rollout is similar yet with richer output fθ(Qt0 , V1:t) (ot0, . . . , ot), with oτ = rτ , cτ , aτ , respond or remain silent, request clarification or feedback, request user execution. (2) Unlike passive streaming, interactive streaming maintains an evolving interaction history Ht. At later decision time τ > t, new interaction Hτ updates this state: Hτ = Update(Ht, Hτ ), (3) where Hτ may correspond to new user query that adds, cancels, or modifies request, user feedback that resolves previous clarification request ct, or newly observed evidence resulting from an execution request at. With the updated state and retained interaction history, the model continues with similar streaming processing fθ(Hτ , V1:τ ) Oτ :τ , τ τ. (4) This process unfolds along shared arrow of time, where both the user and model can initiate interaction, update one another, and continue acting on the evolving video stream. Interactive streaming thus enables bidirectional communication within single continuous trajectory.

sections.title: 3.2 Interactive Streaming Task Taxonomy
sections.content: As aforementioned, passive streaming models primarily focus on proactive monitoring, while interactive streaming further extends to task coordination and feedback seeking. Accordingly, we briefly introduce the core interactive streaming capabilities across three complementary families. Proactive Monitoring. The user specifies condition to monitor, and the model observes the stream until sufficient evidence supports response: Proactive Timing: The model issues notification when the target condition is first verifiably satisfied, completing the task. Proactive Understanding: The model answers an associated visual question once both the trigger and sufficient answer evidence are available. Repeated Proactiveness: The model maintains the request across multiple occurrences and responds once for each distinct occurrence. Streaming Task Coordination. The model maintains and updates active commitments as user requests evolve or coexist: Task State Update: The user cancels or modifies an existing monitoring task, and the model updates subsequent behavior accordingly. Concurrent Requests: The model handles multiple monitoring objectives or interleaved immediate questions while preserving all remaining active commitments. 4 Figure 2 Construction and composition of ALIVE training data. Top: Targets in public videos are coarsely localized and temporally refined. Grounded evidence guides dialogue synthesis and alignment for proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction, followed by quality verification. Bottom: Task distributions are shown separately for SFT and RL. The donut chart summarizes video-content categories jointly over both training sets. Feedback-Seeking Interaction. When the current context is insufficient to resolve request, the model identifies the missing prerequisite and actively seeks the required feedback: Ask-for-Monitor : When the answer depends on future observations, the model asks whether the user wants to establish monitoring task and responds once the relevant evidence appears. Ask-for-Information: When the request is ambiguous, the model asks for clarification and uses the additional information to resolve the original query. Ask-for-Execution: When necessary visual evidence is unavailable, the model requests concrete user action that reveals the missing information before answering. Across these tasks, the model must preserve valid commitments and incorporate subsequent user feedback or visual evidence into its ongoing interaction state.

sections.title: 3.3 Data Construction and Datasets
sections.content: We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K using public video segments and annotations from diverse sources. These include TimeLens2 [65], LLaVA-Video [62], TimeLens [60], Shot2Story [17], VideoGPT+ [34], VideoRefer-700K [57], QVHighlights [21], Vript [54], WebVid [2], DiDeMo [18], Ref-YouTube-VOS [40], Nymeria [33], EPIC-KITCHENS [7], Charades-Ego [42], Ego4D [14], HoloAssist [45], Ego-Exo4D [15], DenseStep2M [12], COIN [43], HACS [63], Charades-STA [11], STAR [49], ActivityNet [3], and Oops [9]. We pair these video segments with timestamped user requests, feedback, and assistant responses or silence to construct interaction trajectories. As illustrated in Fig. 2, construction proceeds through temporal evidence grounding, dialogue synthesis and alignment, and quality verification. Temporal evidence grounding and refinement. For videos with existing descriptions and approximate timestamps, we use them to identify candidate intervals; otherwise, an offline MLLM first detects relevant targets and coarsely localizes their occurrence. We then refine each candidate using an offline MLLM with access to video context both before and after the candidate event. This bidirectional temporal context helps identify the earliest sampled time at which the required visual condition is met, such as entity recognizability, text readability, scene visibility, or action completion. Dialogue synthesis and temporal alignment. Given grounded targets and timestamps, we synthesize dialogues that pair user requests with appropriate assistant responses and, where needed, task updates or feedback 5 exchanges. We align these exchanges with the evolving task state and visual evidence, so that each answer follows the observations or user feedback needed to support it. Quality verification. We verify two aspects of each example. Interaction-strategy validity: the selected strategy must be appropriate for the current task state and information gap, and any requested clarification, action, or continued observation must be relevant to resolving the request. Causal answerability: each answer must be supported by the video observed up to its assigned timestamp and the preceding interaction history, without relying on future frames or subsequent user feedback. Examples that fail either check are filtered. Statistics. Through this construction process, we generate ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K, comprising 288,436 and 3,523 interaction examples for supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, respectively. Both datasets span diverse scenarios and cover eight task types across proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. Fig. 2 summarizes the task distributions and video-content categories.

sections.title: 4 Learning Interactive Streaming Video LLMs
sections.content: Streaming interaction requires model to select an appropriate interaction strategy, respond accurately when the necessary evidence becomes available, and remain silent when response is unwarranted. These behaviors depend jointly on visual observations and the evolving interaction history. We train ALIVE in two stages. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning establishes these conditional interaction behaviors, while reinforcement learning further optimizes them on model-generated trajectories through Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment. Output format. At each decision time t, the model generates ot pθ( V1:t, Ht) from the observed video prefix and interaction history. control token indicates whether to respond (R) or remain silent (S). When responding, the subsequent text expresses the appropriate strategy, such as answering directly, proposing continued monitoring, requesting clarification, or asking the user to perform an action. All outputs are generated by single autoregressive model.

sections.title: 4.1 Contrastive Supervised Fine-Tuning
sections.content: The appropriate interaction behavior is not determined by visual content alone. The same observation may warrant different outputs depending on the active request, task status, or available user feedback. We construct two complementary families of controlled contrasts to supervise these dependencies. Response-gate contrasts. We hold the visual prefix and comparison time fixed while varying an interaction condition that changes whether the model should respond. These conditions include query relevance, task status, and feedback state. For example, the same target appearance requires notification under an active monitoring request but silence after cancellation or fulfillment of single-occurrence request. These contrasts provide explicit supervision for warranted responses and critical silence under visually similar conditions. Action-strategy contrasts. We vary evidence availability or referential ambiguity while preserving the underlying task. When sufficient evidence is available, the model should answer directly. An ambiguous reference requires clarification, whereas missing visual evidence may require concrete user action or proposal to continue observing. We pair these situations with their direct-answer counterparts to teach strategy selection according to the information available at the time. Both sides use the response gate, with the distinction learned through supervision on the response text. Interaction-aware training. We convert interaction trajectories into streaming training instances centered on annotated responses. For response at time a, we sample post-response offset δ uniformly from {0, . . . , } and set the instance endpoint to = + δ, capped before the next response or at the trajectory end. Extending instances beyond the response exposes the model to the transition back to silence. For response-gate contrasts, the designated comparison time takes precedence, ensuring that the instance reaches the critical response-or-silence decision. We then retain contiguous visual window ending at e. Its length is sampled uniformly between Nmin and min(Nmax, Te), where Nmin and Nmax specify the minimum and maximum numbers of frames in the sampled Figure 3 Two-stage training of ALIVE. Left: Contrastive SFT uses action-strategy and response-gate pairs to teach how available evidence and interaction history affect the appropriate output. and denote response and silence. Within each sampled window, the final response and all silence tokens receive supervision, while earlier responses are masked. Right: RL with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level advantages with local advantages for strategy selection, task response, and critical silence. Trajectory rewards account for strategy correctness (D), task completion (C), and redundancy (P ), and α weights the local advantage. visual window, and Te is the number of available frames up to e. Histories shorter than Nmin are retained in full. Earlier user messages and substantive assistant responses remain as text-only context. Varying visual context while preserving interaction history helps the model adapt to sliding-window inference. Within each instance, we supervise the final in-window response, including its control token and text, together with all silence tokens within the sampled visual window. Earlier responses serve as context and incur no loss. Each supervised output is conditioned only on the preceding observations and utterances. To balance response and silence supervision, let nR and nS denote their respective numbers of supervised control tokens in batch B. Response control and text tokens receive unit weight, while silence tokens receive weight nR/nS. The SFT objective is LSFT = (cid:80) jB mjwj log pθ(yj x<j) jB mjwj (cid:80) , (5) where mj selects supervised tokens, wj is the corresponding weight, and x<j denotes the preceding multimodal context.

sections.title: 4.2 Reinforcement Learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment
sections.content: SFT establishes interaction behaviors from annotated trajectories. RL further refines these behaviors under histories containing the models own outputs. In multi-turn interaction, however, trajectory may contain both successful and unsuccessful behaviors. Assigning the same trajectory-level advantage to every output provides limited guidance about which interaction requirements were satisfied. We therefore introduce BehaviorAligned Credit Assignment (BACA), which combines trajectory-level advantages with local advantages over annotated behavioral units. Streaming rollouts and trajectory reward. Starting from the SFT policy, we sample trajectories for each training episode. Video observations and user turns are replayed chronologically, and generated outputs become part of the subsequent interaction history. Policy sampling focuses on user turns and temporal regions around annotated response and critical-silence events. Outside these regions, observations continue to update the history while silence is simulated without contributing to the training loss. Annotations guide training-time scheduling and evaluation; the policy observes only the available video and interaction history. 7 Each sampled trajectory τi receives reward Ri = DiCiPi, Pi = exp λ (cid:18) Ki max(1, req ) (cid:19) , (6) where Di evaluates the required interaction strategy and Ci aggregates task completion, accounting for response correctness, timing, and compliance with the current task state, including annotated silence requirements. Semantic correctness is assessed by an LLM judge against the reference requirements. Temporal responses additionally receive credit according to their alignment with the annotated target time. The redundancy penalty factor Pi downweights trajectories with redundant responses, with Ki denoting their count and req the expected response count. Behavioral units. We construct local evaluation units from annotated user turns, response targets, and silence conditions. These units capture three complementary aspects of interaction: strategy selection, which evaluates the appropriateness of the interaction strategy; task response, which evaluates the correctness of answers or notifications and their timing when applicable; and critical silence, which evaluates whether the model refrains from unwarranted responses during designated periods. For pre-event waiting, silence receives local credit only when the subsequent target also receives positive completion credit. behavioral unit may span one or several model calls, including both responses and silence. Its extent is determined by the relevant interaction requirement rather than fixed number of dialogue turns. Corresponding units are aligned across trajectories by their annotation identities, allowing comparison even when sampled trajectories produce different numbers of responses. Each generated call is assigned to at most one local unit. Global and local advantages. sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: We initialize ALIVE from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [1] and apply the two-stage training procedure described in 4. To preserve general question-answering ability and reinforce the decision to answer directly when sufficient evidence is available, we augment ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K with 274K and 800 curated reactive QA examples, respectively. These examples are drawn from LLaVA-Video [62], Molmo2 [6], and Ego4D [14]. In both stages, we freeze the vision encoder and connector and update only the language model. SFT runs for one epoch with batch size of 512 and learning rate of 1 105. Videos are sampled at 1 FPS. For SFT instance construction, we set Nmin = 10, Nmax = 30, and the maximum post-response offset = 4 positions. RL uses = 4 rollouts per episode and α = 1.

5.2 Evaluation Protocols
Public Benchmarks. We evaluate on OVO-Bench [27], StreamingBench [29], IPIBench [24], and ProactiveV-
ideoQA [47] using their original task-specific protocols. We report accuracy (%) for the first three benchmarks
and PAUC for ProactiveVideoQA, with ω = 0.5. We report official results where available. Otherwise, we
adapt each model to the official evaluation code while preserving its native inference settings as closely as
possible. Full task-level results are reported in Table 2.
sections.content: FSI-Bench. To evaluate feedback-seeking interaction in streaming video models (3.2), we introduce FSI-Bench, comprising 1,235 episodes across four tasks: Ask-for-Monitor (AFM, 154), Ask-for-Information (AFI, 446), Ask-for-Execution (AFE, 459), and Direct Answer (DA, 176). The last task tests immediate answering when sufficient evidence is available. We use two protocols at query time t0. The Explicit Decision Protocol (EDP) requires choice among Answer, Wait, and Request, while the Free-form Decision Protocol (FDP) infers this choice from the models natural response using fixed LLM judge. Both use causal video and feedback streams with identical scoring rules. Let d, {0, 0.5, 1} denote initial decision and answer correctness scores, respectively. Decision scoring is binary, except that choosing Wait on AFE receives partial credit (d = 0.5) for deferring an unsupported answer without requesting the required action. Public Benchmarks. We compare ALIVE with VideoLLM-Online [4], Flash-VStream [59], Dispider [37],

with enhanced interactive capabilities, including managing concurrent user tasks and adapting to changes in
their states.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.content: We formulate interactive streaming video understanding around proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction, and introduce ALIVE to support these capabilities. We train the model on ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K through contrastive supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA). ALIVE achieves state-of-the-art overall performance among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong capabilities in both streaming video understanding and interaction. We believe ALIVE provides an empirical foundation for developing multimodal assistants that continuously perceive the world and sustain meaningful interactions with users as their needs evolve. ALIVE remains vision-language model, and enabling spoken interaction requires external automatic speech recognition (ASR) and text-to-speech (TTS) components. Extending this framework to native omni-modal models is promising direction toward more natural streaming interaction across vision, language, and audio.
